\chapter{Cryptography — RSA}
%%% generated by the blueprint pipeline from TCSlib.Cryptography.RSA
%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\section{Overview}

This file develops a small cost-tracking monad \texttt{TimeM T α}, whose values carry both a
return value of type $\alpha$ and an accumulated time cost of type $T$ (typically $T = \bbn$
counting comparisons), together with worked examples (median of three, insertion sort) that
prove functional correctness on the returned value and complexity bounds on the recorded cost.
It then formalizes the RSA cryptosystem: for distinct primes $p,q$ and exponents $e,d$ with
$ed = 1 + k(p-1)(q-1)$, decryption inverts encryption modulo $n = pq$.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Pure computation in the time monad]
\lean{TimeM.pure}
\leanok
Lifts a value $a : \alpha$ into the computation $\langle a, 0\rangle$ of type \texttt{TimeM T α},
i.e.\ the computation that returns $a$ at zero time cost.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Sequential composition in the time monad]
\lean{TimeM.bind}
\leanok
Given $m : \texttt{TimeM T α}$ and $f : \alpha \to \texttt{TimeM T β}$, the bind of $m$ and $f$
runs $f$ on the value returned by $m$ and returns $\langle (f\,m.\mathrm{ret}).\mathrm{ret},\;
m.\mathrm{time} + (f\,m.\mathrm{ret}).\mathrm{time}\rangle$: the two time costs are added.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Return value of \texttt{pure}]
\lean{TimeM.ret_pure}
\leanok
The value returned by $\mathrm{pure}\,a$ is $a$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Return value of a bind]
\lean{TimeM.ret_bind}
\leanok
The value returned by the bind of $m$ with $f$ is the value returned by $f\,m.\mathrm{ret}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Return value of a map]
\lean{TimeM.ret_map}
\leanok
For $f : \alpha \to \beta$ and $x : \texttt{TimeM T α}$, the value returned by the mapped
computation is $f(x.\mathrm{ret})$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Return value of \texttt{seqRight}]
\lean{TimeM.ret_seqRight}
\leanok
The right-sequencing of $x$ and $y$ returns the value returned by $y\,()$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Return value of \texttt{seqLeft}]
\lean{TimeM.ret_seqLeft}
\leanok
The left-sequencing of $x$ and $y$ returns $x.\mathrm{ret}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Return value of \texttt{seq}]
\lean{TimeM.ret_seq}
\leanok
For $f : \texttt{TimeM T (α → β)}$ and $x : \texttt{Unit → TimeM T α}$, the application
$\mathrm{seq}\,f\,x$ returns $f.\mathrm{ret}\bigl((x\,()).\mathrm{ret}\bigr)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Time cost of a bind]
\lean{TimeM.time_bind}
\leanok
The time cost of the bind of $m$ with $f$ is $m.\mathrm{time} + (f\,m.\mathrm{ret}).\mathrm{time}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Time cost of \texttt{pure}]
\lean{TimeM.time_pure}
\leanok
The time cost of $\mathrm{pure}\,a$ is $0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Time cost of a map]
\lean{TimeM.time_map}
\leanok
Mapping a function over a computation does not change its time cost: it is $x.\mathrm{time}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Time cost of \texttt{seqRight}]
\lean{TimeM.time_seqRight}
\leanok
The time cost of the right-sequencing of $x$ and $y$ is $x.\mathrm{time} + (y\,()).\mathrm{time}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Time cost of \texttt{seqLeft}]
\lean{TimeM.time_seqLeft}
\leanok
The time cost of the left-sequencing of $x$ and $y$ is $x.\mathrm{time} + (y\,()).\mathrm{time}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Time cost of \texttt{seq}]
\lean{TimeM.time_seq}
\leanok
The time cost of $\mathrm{seq}\,f\,x$ is $f.\mathrm{time} + (x\,()).\mathrm{time}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Tick]
\lean{TimeM.tick}
\leanok
The computation $\mathrm{tick}\,c$ returns the trivial value and records time cost $c$; it is the
basic way of charging $c$ units of time.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Return value of a tick]
\lean{TimeM.ret_tick}
\leanok
\uses{TimeM.tick}
The value returned by $\mathrm{tick}\,c$ is the unit value.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Time cost of a tick]
\lean{TimeM.time_tick}
\leanok
\uses{TimeM.tick}
The time cost of $\mathrm{tick}\,c$ is $c$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Maximum of two naturals, timed]
\lean{max2}
\leanok
The timed computation returning the larger of two natural numbers $x,y$, charging one unit of
time for the single comparison $x \le y$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Median of three, timed]
\lean{median3}
\leanok
For $a,b,c$ in a linear order, the timed computation returning a median of $a,b,c$ by a nested
sequence of comparisons, charging one unit of time per comparison performed.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Correctness of the timed median]
\lean{median3_correct}
\leanok
\uses{median3}
The value returned by $\mathrm{median3}\,a\,b\,c$ is a median of $a$, $b$, $c$, in the sense that
it lies between at least one of the pairs drawn from $\{a,b,c\}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Comparison count of the timed median]
\lean{median3_time}
\leanok
\uses{median3}
The computation $\mathrm{median3}\,a\,b\,c$ records a time cost of at most $3$, i.e.\ it performs
at most three comparisons.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Timed ordered insertion]
\lean{insert}
\leanok
Inserts $x$ into a list, walking the list until the first element $y$ with $x \le y$ and charging
one unit of time per comparison. On a sorted input it produces the sorted list containing $x$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Timed insertion sort]
\lean{insertionSort}
\leanok
\uses{insert}
Insertion sort in the time monad: recursively sort the tail and then insert the head using the
timed insertion, accumulating the comparisons performed by every insertion step.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Sortedness by adjacent pairs]
\lean{IsSorted}
\leanok
The predicate on lists defined recursively: the empty list and singletons are sorted, and
$x :: y :: \mathit{rest}$ is sorted when $x \le y$ and $y :: \mathit{rest}$ is sorted.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Adjacent sortedness is a chain]
\lean{isSorted_iff_isChain}
\leanok
\uses{IsSorted}
For any list $\mathit{xs}$, the predicate \texttt{IsSorted} holds of $\mathit{xs}$ if and only if
$\mathit{xs}$ is a chain for $\le$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Adjacent sortedness equals pairwise sortedness]
\lean{isSorted_iff_sorted}
\leanok
\uses{IsSorted, isSorted_iff_isChain}
For any list $\mathit{xs}$, the predicate \texttt{IsSorted} holds of $\mathit{xs}$ if and only if
$\mathit{xs}$ is sorted in the usual pairwise sense with respect to $\le$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Value returned by the timed insertion]
\lean{ret_insert}
\leanok
\uses{insert}
The value returned by the timed insertion of $x$ into $\mathit{xs}$ is the ordinary ordered
insertion of $x$ into $\mathit{xs}$ for the relation $\le$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Value returned by the timed insertion sort]
\lean{ret_insertionSort}
\leanok
\uses{insertionSort, ret_insert}
The value returned by the timed insertion sort of $\mathit{xs}$ is the ordinary insertion sort of
$\mathit{xs}$ for the relation $\le$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Length after a timed insertion]
\lean{length_ret_insert}
\leanok
\uses{insert, ret_insert}
The list returned by inserting $x$ into $\mathit{xs}$ has length $\abs{\mathit{xs}} + 1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Length after a timed insertion sort]
\lean{length_ret_insertionSort}
\leanok
\uses{insertionSort, ret_insertionSort}
The list returned by the timed insertion sort of $\mathit{xs}$ has the same length as
$\mathit{xs}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Timed insertion is a permutation]
\lean{insert_perm}
\leanok
\uses{insert, ret_insert}
The list returned by inserting $x$ into $\mathit{xs}$ is a permutation of $x :: \mathit{xs}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Timed insertion preserves sortedness]
\lean{insert_sorted}
\leanok
\uses{IsSorted, insert, isSorted_iff_sorted, ret_insert}
If $\mathit{xs}$ is sorted, then the list returned by inserting $x$ into $\mathit{xs}$ is sorted.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Timed insertion sort is a permutation]
\lean{insertionSort_perm}
\leanok
\uses{insertionSort, ret_insertionSort}
The list returned by the timed insertion sort of $\mathit{xs}$ is a permutation of $\mathit{xs}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Timed insertion sort returns a sorted list]
\lean{insertionSort_sorted}
\leanok
\uses{IsSorted, insertionSort, isSorted_iff_sorted, ret_insertionSort}
For every list $\mathit{xs}$, the list returned by the timed insertion sort is sorted.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Functional correctness of insertion sort]
\lean{insertionSort_correct}
\leanok
\uses{IsSorted, insertionSort, insertionSort_perm, insertionSort_sorted}
For every list $\mathit{xs}$, the output of the timed insertion sort is both sorted and a
permutation of $\mathit{xs}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Insertion sort recurrence]
\lean{timeInsertionSortRec}
\leanok
The worst-case comparison recurrence $T(0) = 0$ and $T(n+1) = T(n) + n$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Cost of one insertion]
\lean{time_insert_le}
\leanok
\uses{insert}
Inserting $x$ into a list $\mathit{xs}$ costs at most $\abs{\mathit{xs}}$ comparisons.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Insertion sort meets its recurrence]
\lean{time_insertionSort_le_rec}
\leanok
\uses{insert, insertionSort, ret_insertionSort, timeInsertionSortRec, time_insert_le}
The time cost recorded by the timed insertion sort of $\mathit{xs}$ is at most
$T(\abs{\mathit{xs}})$, where $T$ is the insertion sort recurrence.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Quadratic bound for the recurrence]
\lean{timeInsertionSortRec_le_sq}
\leanok
\uses{timeInsertionSortRec}
For every $n$, the recurrence satisfies $T(n) \le n^2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Insertion sort performs at most $n^2$ comparisons]
\lean{time_insertionSort_le_sq}
\leanok
\uses{insertionSort, timeInsertionSortRec_le_sq, time_insertionSort_le_rec}
The time cost recorded by the timed insertion sort of a list $\mathit{xs}$ of length $n$ is at
most $n^2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{lemma}[Core RSA exponent identity]
\lean{RSA.rsa_core}
\leanok
Let $p$ be prime. For every $c \in \bbn$ and every $x \in \bbz/p\bbz$,
\[
x^{\,1 + c(p-1)} = x .
\]
This is the form of Fermat's little theorem needed for RSA, valid also at $x = 0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[RSA identity from an exponent factorization]
\lean{RSA.rsa_zmod_of_factor}
\leanok
\uses{RSA.rsa_core}
Let $p$ be prime and $m, ed, c \in \bbn$ with $ed = 1 + c(p-1)$. Then $m^{ed} \equiv m$ in
$\bbz/p\bbz$, where both sides are the images of natural numbers.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[RSA identity modulo $p$]
\lean{RSA.rsa_zmod_p}
\leanok
\uses{RSA.rsa_zmod_of_factor}
If $p$ is prime and $ed = 1 + k(p-1)(q-1)$, then $m^{ed} \equiv m$ in $\bbz/p\bbz$ for every
$m \in \bbn$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[RSA identity modulo $q$]
\lean{RSA.rsa_zmod_q}
\leanok
\uses{RSA.PublicKey, RSA.rsa_zmod_of_factor}
If $q$ is prime and $ed = 1 + k(p-1)(q-1)$, then $m^{ed} \equiv m$ in $\bbz/q\bbz$ for every
$m \in \bbn$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Combining the two factors by CRT]
\lean{RSA.rsa_crt}
\leanok
\uses{RSA.PublicKey}
Let $p$ and $q$ be coprime and suppose $m^{ed} \equiv m$ both in $\bbz/p\bbz$ and in
$\bbz/q\bbz$. Then $m^{ed} \equiv m$ in $\bbz/pq\bbz$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[CRT combination in power form]
\lean{RSA.rsa_crt_pow}
\leanok
\uses{RSA.PublicKey, RSA.rsa_crt}
The same statement written with the power taken inside the quotient ring: if $p$ and $q$ are
coprime and $\bar m^{\,ed} = \bar m$ in $\bbz/p\bbz$ and in $\bbz/q\bbz$, then
$\bar m^{\,ed} = \bar m$ in $\bbz/pq\bbz$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{definition}[RSA public key]
\lean{RSA.PublicKey}
\leanok
A public key consists of a modulus $n \in \bbn$ and a public exponent $e \in \bbn$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[RSA secret key]
\lean{RSA.SecretKey}
\leanok
\uses{RSA.PublicKey}
A secret key consists of a public key together with naturals $p, q, d, k$ and proofs that $p$ and
$q$ are prime, that $p \ne q$, that the public modulus satisfies $n = pq$, and that the exponents
satisfy $e d = 1 + k(p-1)(q-1)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[RSA encryption]
\lean{RSA.encrypt}
\leanok
\uses{RSA.PublicKey}
Encryption of a message $m \in \bbn$ under a public key is $\bar m^{\,e} \in \bbz/n\bbz$, using
only the public data.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[RSA decryption]
\lean{RSA.decrypt}
\leanok
\uses{RSA.SecretKey}
Decryption of a ciphertext $c \in \bbz/n\bbz$ under a secret key is $c^{\,d}$, where $d$ is the
private exponent.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Correctness of RSA]
\lean{RSA.rsa_correctness}
\leanok
\uses{RSA.SecretKey, RSA.decrypt, RSA.encrypt, RSA.rsa_crt_pow, RSA.rsa_zmod_p, RSA.rsa_zmod_q}
For any secret key and any message $m \in \bbn$, decrypting the encryption of $m$ recovers $m$:
\[
\bigl(\bar m^{\,e}\bigr)^{d} = \bar m \quad \text{in } \bbz/n\bbz .
\]
\end{theorem}
